Sensitive microwave detectors are important for wireless communications [1], nondestructive security screening [2], medical imaging [3], electronic countermeasures [4], and searches for high-frequency gravitational
waves [5, 6] and the electromagnetic signatures of ultralight dark matter [7 - 10]. High-fidelity detection of weak
signals at the energy scale of a single microwave photon remains a major challenge [11 - 13]. Thermal noise
limits the sensitivity of conventional metal-antenna microwave receivers to about 10−21 W/
√
Hz [14].
Several newer devices have been developed for weak microwave signals.
Graphene self-switching diodes have
a noise-equivalent power (NEP) of approximately 2.2 ×
10−9 W/
√
Hz [15].
Rydberg-atom microwave superheterodyne receivers have achieved an electric-field sensitivity of approximately 55 nV cm−1/
√
Hz [16]. Although
these approaches improve weak-signal detection, reaching
the single-microwave-photon energy scale remains challenging. Cryogenic operation reduces thermal noise and
can substantially improve microwave detection sensitivity.
Among cryogenic detectors based on semiconductors, graphene, and superconducting devices [17 - 21],
Josephson-junction (JJ) detectors offer strong nonlinearity and controllable phase dynamics [22, 23].
JJbased microwave detection schemes fall broadly into two

classes.
In the first, a superconducting qubit registers a state change induced by a single microwave photon [24 - 26]. Coupling the qubit to a microwave resonator
typically converts the incident traveling photon into a
standing-wave cavity mode, strengthening its interaction
with the qubit. Under dispersive coupling, a cavity photon shifts the qubit transition frequency, which can be
read out to detect the photon. The overall efficiency depends on photon injection, qubit decoherence, and statereadout fidelity.
The frequency-matching requirements
of the cavity and qubit typically constrain the operating bandwidth.
The second class uses voltage switching in a current-biased JJ to detect weak microwave signals [27 - 29]. A junction operated in this regime is termed
a Josephson threshold detector (JTD). The bias current
and the high-frequency current induced by the incident
microwave signal can jointly switch the junction from the
zero-voltage state to a finite-voltage state. In the tiltedwashboard picture, this switch corresponds to the escape
of the phase particle from a potential well. The observed
voltage switch serves as the detection signal. This mechanism allows broadband operation because it does not require precise matching to a narrow cavity mode. The induced current also depends on signal strength or photon
number, giving JTDs the potential for photon-number
resolution (PNR).
Thermal noise limits JTD sensitivity even at millikelvin temperatures, making it difficult to reach the
energy scale of a single microwave photon. Further cooling offers limited practical scope for improving sensitivity at these operating temperatures. We therefore seek
to use the intrinsic nonlinear dynamics of the JTD to

2
lessen the impact of thermal noise while preserving or enhancing the microwave response. In earlier work [30], we
found that a rapid bias-current sweep places a JTD in a
nonequilibrium phase regime that is less sensitive to thermal noise and more responsive to weak microwave signals, potentially reaching the single-photon energy scale.
The method relies on transient oscillations set by the
initial junction phase, which decay through internal dissipation. It therefore requires both a junction with very
low damping (or a very high quality factor Q) and a very
fast current sweep. Our feasibility analysis indicated that
available JTDs did not meet the device parameters used
in that study. In addition, copper-powder and resistor - 
capacitor (RC) low-pass filters installed on the bias line
to suppress environmental noise can have cutoff frequencies as low as approximately 2 kHz [31, 32], which limits
the achievable sweep rate.
These results motivate a way to sustain nonequilibrium
operation with experimentally accessible damping and
bias-current sweep rates. We propose threshold detection
of weak microwave signals using a high-frequency fluxpumped direct-current superconducting quantum interference device (DC-SQUID). The external flux drives a
circulating current, continuously sustaining nonequilibrium phase dynamics throughout the bias-current sweep.
This sustained motion replaces the dissipatively decaying
oscillations initiated by the single junction's initial phase
in our prior work [30]. The scheme can operate at moderate sweep rates and damping. Separate lines carry the
high-frequency flux drive and the current sweep, allowing
their filters and passbands to be designed independently.
This arrangement makes it easier to exploit nonequilibrium phase dynamics experimentally.
Section II develops the resistively and capacitively
shunted junction (RCSJ) model [33] for the flux-driven
DC-SQUID. Using common-mode and differential-mode
phases, we examine how the drive modulates the instantaneous potential and phase dynamics, characterize nonequilibrium motion, and describe how to calculate switching-current distributions (SCDs) and quantify their separability with and without a microwave signal.
Section III examines the effects of DC flux bias,
the amplitude and frequency of the high-frequency flux
drive, and thermal noise, then evaluates sensitivity to
continuous-wave and pulsed microwave signals under optimized drive conditions.

abstract: Superconducting vortex represents a topological entity in type-II superconductors, where the prototypical manifestation of such a macroscopic quantum state holds great promise for applications in future quantum technologies. Deterministic control of the vortex dynamics at the nanoscale is central to enhance superconductors' critical thresholds and design next-generation superconducting quantum devices. However, it is still scientifically challenging due to the intrinsic nature of the vortex pinning landscapes in superconductors. Here, we observe an even-in-field Hall-like signal with about two order of magnitude enhancement in a type-II superconductor/chiral magnet heterostructure, which confines to the field-temperature window where the flux flow coexists with magnetic skyrmions. The polarity of such a giant even-in-field transverse response reverses between orthogonal current directions, suggesting an on-track vortex flow driven by a nematic fluxon - skyrmion interaction analyzed via the extended vortex-viscosity tensor. More critically, a deterministic manipulation of skyrmions at the nanoscale within the hybrid system enables selective and reversible controls over the dissipative behavior and therefore the reconfigurable fluxon transport, mimic the precise control of curling stone in winter Olympic, thereby opening a new avenue towards the exploration of programmable topological and superconducting quantum devices.

Superconducting vortex represents a topological entity in type-II superconductors, 
where the prototypical manifestation of such a macroscopic quantum state holds great 
promise for applications in future quantum technologies. Deterministic control of the 
vortex dynamics at the nanoscale is central to enhance superconductors' critical 
thresholds and design next-generation superconducting quantum devices. However, it 
is still scientifically challenging due to the intrinsic nature of the vortex pinning 
landscapes in superconductors. Here, we observe an even-in-field Hall-like signal with 
about two order of magnitude enhancement in a type-II superconductor/chiral magnet 
heterostructure, which confines to the field-temperature window where the flux flow 
coexists with magnetic skyrmions. The polarity of such a giant even-in-field transverse 
response reverses between orthogonal current directions, suggesting an on-track vortex 
flow driven by a nematic fluxon - skyrmion interaction analyzed via the extended 
vortex-viscosity tensor. More critically, a deterministic manipulation of skyrmions at 
the nanoscale within the hybrid system enables selective and reversible controls over 
the dissipative behavior and therefore the reconfigurable fluxon transport, mimic the 
precise control of curling stone in winter Olympic, thereby opening a new avenue 
towards the exploration of programmable topological and superconducting quantum 
devices.

3 
In type-II superconductors, a superconducting vortex is a quantized filament 
comprising a normal-state core and surrounding supercurrents1,2. Traditionally 
engineered pinning landscapes have long been used to suppress vortex motion, mitigate 
dissipation, and enhance critical superconducting thresholds3,4. Today, precise and 
reversible manipulation of vortex is a prerequisite for developing vortex-based quantum 
technologies5-9, with potential applications in vortex-based memory cells6, quantum 
sensing10, topological quantum computing7,8, etc. Vortex dynamics reflect a force 
balance among the current-induced driving force, the transverse Magnus force, and the 
viscous drag force, where the vortex velocity deviates only slightly from the direction 
of Lorentz force in conventional superconductors (Magnus coefficient is much less than 
vortex viscosity)11,12, as shown in Fig. 1a. This drag is inherently dissipative in 
superconductors, while its microscopic mechanism remains heavily debated over past 
60 years11, spanning Bardeen-Stephen quasiparticle currents12, Anderson phase 
slips13,14, and spectral flow models15,16. Steering vortex at the nanoscale remains 
formidable because conventional pinning landscapes17 and the fixed interfacial 
symmetry18 are established after material growth or device fabrication, so that the 
vortex cannot be reconfigured during operations19. Thus, realizing efficient and 
programmable fluxonic devices requires a paradigm shift to actively rewritable 
landscapes capable of spatial and reversible modulation of the vortex viscosity17,20. 
 
An effective route to reshape vortex dynamic may be achieved by constructing a 
coupling of vortex with other particles10 or quasiparticles21: phonon22, magnon23 or

4 
photon24, even including topological quasiparticles such as skyrmions25 etc., which 
have enabled to probe and reconfigure vortex as an active elements in hybrid quantum 
systems10,21-26. Among them, magnetic skyrmions are topologically stable quasiparticle 
with chiral and gradient spin textures that can be deterministically created, moved and 
annihilated at nanoscale27-32. Over the past decade, the interplay between these 
topological magnetic and superconducting entities has inspired predictions of emergent 
static composite states33-36, notably topological superconductivity37 and Majorana zero 
modes38,39, etc. Beyond those static ones, the nanoscale spin gradient of a skyrmion 
could play critical roles in their dynamics36,40: it may experience an unforeseeable 
exchange-mediated drag channel when a superconducting vortex moving across a 
magnetic skyrmion, as illustrated in Fig. 1b, offering both a fresh window on the 
dissipation landscape and a rewritable knob for controlling vortex motion. However, 
despite quite a few studies attempt to locally probe the interplay of skyrmions and 
vortices25,33-36,40,41, the effective control of the Abrikosov vortex (or fluxon) transport 
and emergent quantum phenomena has been largely hindered by the limitation of largearea stabilized skyrmion phase within wide windows of temperature and magnetic 
field42. 
 
In this work, we construct an artificial hybrid quantum heterostructure consisted of a 
strongly correlated half-metallic ferromagnet La0.67Sr0.33MnO3 (LSMO) and a type-II 
superconducting Nb thin film. This ferromagnet provides a brand-new platform to hold 
a large-area stable skyrmion (SkX) phase within wide ranges of temperature/magnetic

5 
field43. In the superconducting transition regime of this hybrid system, we observe a 
two order of magnitude enhancement of an even-in-field Hall-like signal. The reversed 
polarity of this giant transverse response between orthogonal current directions 
provides a direct signature of a nematic vortex-skyrmion interaction. Ultimately, we 
demonstrate the precise manipulation of individual skyrmions, thereby affording 
selective and reversible control over the vortex dynamics at nanoscale. 
 
An even transverse response in the type-II superconductor-chiral 
magnet hybrid system 
To investigate the dynamics of superconducting vortex in the hybrid system, we 
fabricated the Hall bars from a Nb (70 nm) film and Nb (70 nm)/LSMO bilayers. A 
large-area skyrmion phase over a broad range of temperature and magnetic field can be 
stabilized in the 150-nm LSMO (SkX) layer43. In comparison, we prepared identical 
Hall bars from a Nb/LSMO bilayer with a 15-nm LSMO without skyrmions (nonSkX)43. The superconducting behaviors of the above samples can be seen in Fig. S2, 
indicating the nature of high-quality superconducting layers in the hybrid system. 
Details of the thin-film growth, device fabrication, domain imaging, and transport 
measurements are provided in Supplementary Section 1. Structural and roomtemperature magnetic characterization are shown in Supplementary Fig. S1 and Section 
2, while superconducting transitions and transport in Nb/non-SkX are provided in 
Supplementary Figs. S2 and S3 and Section 3 and Section 4.

6 
The longitudinal (𝜌௫௫) and transverse (𝜌௫௬) resistivities of the devices were measured 
at 7.6 K, as schematically shown in Figs. 2a and 2b. Distinct from the 𝜌௫௫ and 𝜌௫௬ in 
the bare Nb film (Fig. 2c), we observe a giant Hall-like signal exhibiting the same 
polarity for both positive and negative magnetic fields within the superconducting 
transition regime of the Nb/SkX hybrid system as seen in Fig. 2d. Such an even-in-field 
transverse response represents a symmetry forbidden in conventional Hall effect. 
Crucially, this anomalous signal is entirely absent in both the bare Nb and Nb/non-SkX 
samples (grey zones in Figs. 2c, S3b), and its maximum amplitude of the Hall-like 
signal in the Nb/SkX system is nearly two orders of magnitude larger than that of the 
bare Nb film. 
 
To visually correlate these transport anomalies with the underlying topological 
magnetic textures, we employed cryogenic magnetic force microscopy (MFM) to 
image the real-space domain evolution. The low lower-critical field of the thin Nb layer 
allows the fringing fields of the ferromagnetic domains to be resolved directly through 
the superconductor. As seen in Fig. 2e, the number of negatively oriented skyrmions 
gradually increase as the decrease of magnetic field (A→B→C); when the direction of 
magnetic field reverses, the negatively oriented domains then switch into positive ones 
(D→E); finally, further increase of the reversed magnetic field results in the 
progressively diminish of the positively oriented skyrmions (F→G→H). Strikingly, a 
comparative analysis of the transport data and MFM images (Figs. 2d and e) reveals 
that the giant even-in-field 𝜌௫௬ emerges exclusively in the superconducting transition

7 
regime where skyrmions are present. Furthermore, in stark contrast to the Nb and 
Nb/non-SkX references, this giant even-in field 𝜌௫௬ in Nb/SkX varies nonmonotonically with increasing temperature (7.4~8.6 K) and is confined to the existing 
window of non-zero topological Hall effect (THE)43, where the LSMO layer hosts 
large-area skyrmion phase, as seen in Fig. S4. Together, these observations tie the 
anomalous transverse response to the coexistence of superconducting vortices and 
magnetic skyrmions. 
 
Skyrmion nematicity imprints anisotropic vortex dissipation 
To pin down the microscopic mechanism that derives this giant even-in-field transverse 
Hall-like signal, we examine the scaling relationship between 𝜌௫௫ and 𝜌௫௬ within the 
superconducting transition regime. Power-law fits (|𝜌௫௬| ∝𝜌௫௫
௄) yield exponents of 
𝐾ൌ1.03~1.19 for temperature sweeps at fixed magnetic fields (Fig. 3a) and 𝐾ൌ
0.82~0.88 for field sweeps at fixed temperatures (Fig. S5). The corresponding 
isothermal-field sweeps and fixed-field temperature sweeps are provided in 
Supplementary Figs. S4, S6 - S8 of Supplementary Sections 5 and 6. These values 
drastically deviate from 𝐾ൎ2 which typifies thermally activated flux-flow Hall 
transport in superconductors44. Instead, the scaling 𝐾ൎ1 implies that the transverse 
signal is strictly proportional to 𝜌௫௫ itself. This linear relationship is the hallmark of a 
resistivity-anisotropy (planar-Hall-like) origin rather than a genuine Hall channel. To 
rigorously test this in-plane anisotropy, we fabricated two orthogonal Hall bars aligned 
along the ሾ100ሿ௉஼ and ሾ010ሿ௉஼ crystallographic directions of LSMO on the same

8 
Nb/SkX hybrid system. As shown in Fig. 3b, the even signal exhibits a stark polarity 
reversal between these orthogonal current directions at 8.4 K. Moreover, the Hall 
response is substantially reduced when the current is applied along the ሾ110ሿ௉஼ 
direction (Fig. S9a and b). Notably, neither the bare Nb nor the Nb/non-SkX films 
exhibit any even-in-field Hall-like signal and in-plane anisotropy (Fig. S9c and d). The 
sign reversal of the field-even transverse response upon a 90° rotation of the current 
direction is incompatible with an isotropic in-plane transport response. This 
macroscopic transport anisotropy prompts us to investigate the intrinsic geometric 
structure and spin gradient of the skyrmions. Detailed real-space MFM imaging (Fig. 
3c) reveals that the skyrmions in the bare 150-nm LSMO are inherently elliptical. The 
ratio of their diameters along 30∘ and 120∘ (relative to the ሾ100ሿ௉஼ axis) is 1.25 േ
0.25, with their long axes consistently aligned along 30∘. The elliptical skyrmions are 
largely dictated by the strain-driven magnetic anisotropy and the anisotropic 
Dzyaloshinskii - Moriya interactions43,45,46, establishing a robust nematic order within 
the skyrmion lattice. 
 
Taken together, these observations suggest a compelling physical picture: the 
underlying skyrmions imprint their nematic order directly onto the superconducting 
vortex system. Specifically, interfacial exchange coupling between the normal-state 
vortex core and the anisotropic spin gradient in skyrmions renders the vortex viscosity 
strongly direction-dependent ( 𝜂௔്

interaction. As illustrated in Fig. 3d, the anisotropic force-balance model gives the

9

viscosity axis (see Supplementary Information Section 10 for the full force-balance 
derivation):

through its sin(2θ) dependence, directly accounting for Figs. 2d and 3b. The full forcebalance derivation, phenomenological fits, and comparison in theories are provided in 
Supplementary Section 10. This single framework elegantly accounts for the above 
giant even-in-field Hall-like signal (Fig. 2d), both the anomalous scaling exponent (Fig. 
3a) and the orthogonal polarity reversal (Fig. 3b). Crucially, trivial origins for a fieldeven transverse voltage - such as contact misalignment, 𝑇௖ inhomogeneity, or a 
parallel conduction channel through the metallic LSMO - can be definitively ruled out: 
such artifacts would manifest equally in the identically fabricated Nb and Nb/non-SkX 
samples (Figs. S3 and S9), and fundamentally cannot produce a systematic sign reversal 
upon 90° rotation or respond dynamically to skyrmion density. Additionally, the 
reversal of polarity in the transverse response between the field-down and field-up 
sweeps (Fig. S10) is consistent with Bean critical-state hysteresis: reversing the sweep 
direction reverses the critical-state flux-density gradient and the associated shielding-

10 
current direction, thereby reconfiguring the net vortex motion (see Supplementary Note 
Section 10.4 for details). 
 
Furthermore, to unequivocally distinguish interfacial exchange coupling from purely 
magnetostatic interactions (stray field), we performed control experiments by inserting 
a 2-nm insulating MgO barrier between the Nb and SkX layers. Although this ultrathin 
barrier leaves the stray fields virtually unperturbed, it completely suppresses interfacial 
exchange, thereby entirely eliminating the even transverse response (Fig. S11). This 
critical observation confirms that the nematic fluxon-skyrmion interaction is driven 
intrinsically by interlayer exchange coupling. Thus, we understand that the vortex 
motion in the coupled fluxon - skyrmion system can be deterministically controlled by 
three experimental knobs: current orientation, sweep direction, and temperature within 
the SkX window, and more critically, the skyrmion itself provides a locally rewritable 
landscape, opening a route towards spatially programmable fluxonics. 
 
Reconfigurable fluxon transport by skyrmion writing 
This comprehensive understanding of the nematic fluxon-skyrmion interaction offers 
an unprecedented opportunity: the on-demand tailoring of superconducting dissipation 
and vortex dynamics using skyrmions as programmable control knobs at nanoscale. As 
schematically shown in Fig. 4a, stray field from a scanning MFM tip has been adopted 
to accurately write and move skyrmions in the Nb/SkX hybrid system. The detailed 
control of skyrmions using scanning MFM tip are provided in method section and

11 
elsewhere30. With such a powerful strategy, we carry out the in-situ transport 
measurements combining the magnetic tip writing and imaging as shown in the 
schematic of Fig. 4b. Remarkably, the magnitude of the anomalous Hall-like response 
scales linearly with the number of newly "written" skyrmions. This phenomenon 
provides unequivocal evidence that locally generated topological spin textures directly 
translates to a programmable modulation of the macroscopic vortex dissipation and 
fluxon transport. 
 
Pushed to its ultimate limit, this concept can allow the density, spatial position, and 
even ordering arrangement of skyrmions to precisely manipulate superconducting 
vortex trajectories (Fig. 4c). We have also successfully used the MFM tip to precisely 
displace individual skyrmions within the hybrid device (Fig. 4d). Because the 
anisotropic drag landscape is intrinsically bound to the skyrmions themselves, 
relocating a skyrmion fundamentally shifts the localized friction experienced by nearby 
moving vortex. This reversible and real-space reconfigurability allows superconducting 
fluxons to be deterministically steered with a precision akin to that of an Olympic 
curling stone guided on ice, where locally brushing the ice surface dictates the trajectory. 
Consequently, this discovery establishes a conceptual shift in vortex physics from 
suppressing vortex motion to program it on demand, thereby converting vortex 
dynamics from an unavoidable and uncontrolled source of dissipation into an actively 
reconfigurable degree of freedom which could be a prerequisite for fluxonic quantum 
devices8,9,20. We consider that electrical transport in various cutting-edge designed

12 
superconducting devices based on our hybrid system may provide not only a 
microscopic probe of emergent topological states such as braidable fluxon-skyrmion 
excitations39, but also selective and reversible programme of macroscopic quantum 
coherence for integratable quantum devices7,8,47,48.

Oscillatory 
superconducting proximity effects in 
ferromagnets are conventionally described using the 
diffusive Usadel equation [54]. In this limit, the induced 
pair correlation has a damped-oscillatory form Ψ(x) ∝ 
exp(−x/ξF)cos(x/ξF) [16], where 𝜉𝐹
⬚= √
2ℏ𝐷⬚

⬚ describes 
the decay and oscillation lengths. This simple expression 
illustrates how an exchange field causes superconducting 
correlations to decay in an oscillatory fashion and can 
therefore account qualitatively for a nonmonotonic 
thickness dependence. However, the relevant exchangesplitted Pt thickness must be only approximately 2 nm, 
substantially smaller than the estimated mean free path of 
𝑙mfp= 5 nm [55], while the largest investigated thicknesses 
are comparable to 𝑙mfp. In addition, the induced spin 
splitting is sufficiently strong that complete momentum 
isotropization before appreciable exchange-induced phase 
accumulation cannot be assumed. We therefore use the 
linearized Eilenberger equation as a more accurate 
description of the thickness dependence. Unlike the 
Usadel approximation, this treatment retains the angular 
dependence of the quasiparticle trajectories and remains 
applicable across the crossover between quasiballistic and 
diffusive transport. 
The Eilenberger equation is solved numerically 
using a half-space model for an effective exchange-split Pt 
region. The superconducting correlations are injected at 
the NbN/Pt boundary, while the Pt/Py interface is assumed 
to be transmitting and strongly dephasing, so that coherent 
return from Py is neglected. Elastic impurity scattering is 
included self-consistently through the complete angular 
average of the anomalous Green function (see 
Supplemental Information). Similarly to the oscillation of 
Tc in SC/FM with the FM thickness [16], we use the 
superconducting singlet amplitude as a representative 
physical quantity, correlated here to the loss of available 
Pt electronic density of state for FMR spin-pumping 
damping below Tc. This choice is further motivated by the 
strong spin-orbit impurity scattering in Pt, which 
preferentially relaxes triplet correlations while leaving 
conventional isotropic 𝑠-wave singlet correlations without 
a direct spin-orbit relaxation term [56]. The result for the 
superconducting singlet amplitude is shown in Fig. 3 for a 
spin-splitting Δex = 100 meV and demonstrates good 
agreement with the experimental measurements, capturing 
the experimentally observed rapid suppression and first 
oscillation. The latest Δex value is consistent with both the 
experimental values of Pt moment at Pt/Py interface, 0.22 
µB/at [15] and of Pt exchange-field at Pt/Co interface, 170 
meV [57]. It is important to note here that the comparison 
between the experimental data and the theoretical curve is 
only meaningful for Pt thickness lower than 3 nm, where 
most of Pt is exchange-splitted. The model cannot account 
for the suppression of Δα𝑆
𝑃𝑡/α𝑠𝑝
𝑃𝑡 for Pt thickness larger 
than 5 nm (> 𝑙𝑠𝑑
𝑃𝑡) which is due to the loss of spin 
information inside the Pt so that the NbN superconductive 
transition has no impact on the FMR damping. 
In conclusion, using broadband FMR, we 
investigated the influence of superconductivity on spin 
pumping in NbN/Pt/Py and NbN/Cu/Py trilayers. The 
superconducting transition of NbN reduces the magnetic 
damping by Δα𝑆
𝐶𝑢 and Δα𝑆
𝑃𝑡 respectively, revealing the 
transmission of superconducting correlations through the 
metallic interlayer, and so a reduction of available DOS at 
the Fermi level for spin-pumping. As the Cu interlayer 
thickness increases in NbN/Cu/Py, the relative damping 
reduction Δα𝑆
𝐶𝑢/α𝑠𝑝
𝐶𝑢 first drops to 40%, possibly due to

interfacial scattering, and then only exhibits a weakly 
thickness-dependent behavior consistent with the long 
coherence length of Cu. On the contrary, in NbN/Pt/Py, 
the initial drop is part of a damped oscillatory behavior 
which is suppressed when Cu is intercalated between the 
Pt and Py layers. This behavior is consistent with 
quasiclassical models of exchange-induced oscillatory 
superconducting correlations and associated spectral 
modifications in Pt. More broadly, our results establish 
spin-pumping spectroscopy as a sensitive probe of 
superconducting correlations in buried metallic layers and 
provide microscopic insights relevant to superconducting 
spintronics and the development of nonreciprocal 
superconducting devices.

Section S2 : Critical temperature measurements 
The critical temperature 𝑇𝑐 of the samples was measured by two methods : either magnetic moments as a function 
of temperature 𝑚(𝑇) or resistance as a function of temperature 𝑅(𝑇). Fig. S2.1. shows the critical temperature 
measured for the two types of samples either with Pt or Cu. The critical temperature does not change from sample 
to sample and is estimated at 14.6 ± 0.4 𝐾 and thus the superconducting gap energy of NbN is the similar in the 
whole set of samples. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
FIG S2.1. Critical temperature 𝑻𝒄 as a function the Pt or Cu interlayer thickness in 
NbN/Cu/Py (red square), NbN/Pt/Py (blue triangle) and NbN/Pt/Cu(5)/Py (green circle).

𝑚(𝑇) measurements method: 
m(T) measurements were performed with a QD-Magnetometer MPMS3 SQUID (Superconducting Quantum 
Interference Device). The protocol measurement is as follows : 
1) Degaussing (field reset) : Before each series of low field measurements, the residual field of the 
superconducting magnet is minimized using Oscillate mode (oscillate-to-zero). The field is increased to 
1T and then reduced to 0T in oscillation mode. It is subsequently increased to 2 mT and again reduced to 
0T in oscillation mode. This procedure minimizes the remanent field (trapped flux) and brings the system 
as close as possible to 𝐻= 0𝑇. 
2) Zero Field Cooling (ZFC) : At 𝐻= 0𝑇, the temperature is lowered to 𝑇𝑖 well below the critical 
temperature of the superconductor (for instance 𝑇𝑖= 3𝐾 for Fig. S2.2). 
3) Application of the measurement field : In the out-of-plane (OOP) geometry where the magnetic field 
is applied perpendicular to the plane of the thin film, demagnetization effects are particularly significant 
: the internal demagnetizing field can exceed the applied field by several orders of magnitude. Therefore, 
a low magnetic field 𝐻⊥= 0.2 𝑚𝑇 is applied in order to remain predominantly in the Meissner state. 
4) ZFC Warming (red curve on Fig. S2.2) : The m(T) curve is measured upon warming from 𝑇𝑖 to 𝑇𝑓>
𝑇𝑐. 
5) FC Cooling (blue curve on Fig. S2.2) : Without changing the applied field, m(T) is then measured upon 
cooling from 𝑇𝑓 to 𝑇𝑖. 
The ZFC Warming and FC Cooling measurements were carried out in sweep mode. The temperature was varied 
at a constant rate (0.5 K/min) while the magnetic moment is measured continuously throughout the temperature 
ramp. The critical temperature 𝑇𝑐 is determined graphically as the temperature at which the diamagnetic response 
disappears on the ZFC Warming curve. The associated uncertainty, indicated by the black dashed lines in Fig. 
S2.c., is dominated by the graphical determination, the temperature resolution, and the width of the transition; it is 
estimated to be ±0.2𝐾.
